objective: By the end of this lesson you can explain when and why a pilot must get down fast, pick the configuration and the highest allowable airspeed from the structural limits of your airplane, and fly an emergency descent in a 30 to 45 degree bank to commercial standards (airspeed +0/-10 knots, level-off within 100 feet) with a smooth, well-led recovery.
why: Fire, smoke, a loss of pressurization or a sick occupant can make every minute at altitude dangerous, and the only fix is to get down as fast as the airframe allows [[24:357|AFH 18-8]] [[1:197|PHAK 7-37]]. The hard part is that the fastest descent lives right next to the structural limits, so a commercial pilot has to know exactly where those limits are and why [[1:134|PHAK 5-37]].

prereading.what: Emergency descents, then engine, electrical and cabin fires. Read this twice.
prereading.label: AFH 18-8 to 18-10

prereading.what: Kinds of descents, the typical emergency descent configuration, and the level-off lead rule.
prereading.label: AFH 3-21

warmup: Think first: the AFH tells you to fly the emergency descent at the maximum allowable airspeed, but the commercial ACS gives you a tolerance of +0/-10 knots. In bumpy air the airspeed needle swings several knots each way. So what speed would you actually aim for, and which limit sets it?

key_terms.def: A maneuver to get down as fast as possible, to a lower altitude or to the ground, without exceeding any structural limit [[24:357|AFH 18-8]].
The ratio of the lift the wings make to the airplane's weight, stated in G. A load factor of 3 puts three times the weight on the structure [[1:130|PHAK 5-33]].
The highest load expected in normal operation [[1:130|PHAK 5-33]]. The structure must carry it without detrimental permanent deformation [[60:107|14 CFR 23.2235]].
The limit load times a 1.5 factor of safety [[60:106|14 CFR 23.2230]]. The structure must support it [[60:107|14 CFR 23.2235]], though parts may bend or twist [[1:130|PHAK 5-33]].
A graph of airspeed against load factor that shows the safe envelope for one airplane at a given weight and altitude [[1:134|PHAK 5-37]].
Never-exceed speed, the red line. Above it, structural damage or failure may result. It is set for smooth air only [[1:211|PHAK 8-9]] [[1:134|PHAK 5-37]].
Maximum structural cruising speed, the top of the green arc. Exceed it only in smooth air [[1:211|PHAK 8-9]].
Design maneuvering speed, the rough-air speed. It goes down as weight goes down [[24:389|AFH G-17]] [[1:212|PHAK 8-10]].
VLE is the top speed with the landing gear extended; VFE is the top speed with the flaps extended [[1:212|PHAK 8-10]] [[1:211|PHAK 8-9]].
The pressurization system cannot hold its designed pressure difference, from a malfunction or structural damage [[1:196|PHAK 7-36]].
The longest time you can make and carry out life-saving decisions at an altitude without supplemental oxygen [[1:426|PHAK 17-4]].
Managing every resource on board and outside the airplane, such as ATC, to reach a good outcome [[1:43|PHAK 2-4]].

chunks.title: The emergency descent at commercial standards

body.p: An emergency descent gets the airplane down as soon and as fast as possible, to a lower altitude or to the ground, while staying inside every structural limit [[24:357|AFH 18-8]]. Uncontrollable fire, a sudden loss of cabin pressure, or anything else that demands an immediate, rapid descent can call for it [[24:357|AFH 18-8]].

The picture shows the shape of it: a steep, descending turn. In training you fly it as a turn so you can check for traffic below and look for a place to land, and you start with about 30 to 45 degrees of bank to keep the load factor positive [[24:357|AFH 18-8]].

head: What the examiner checks
Commercial ACS standard
rows: Clear the area (S1)
Clear the area before and during the descent (ACS CA.IX.A.S1)
Airspeed and configuration (S2)
Right for the scenario the examiner gives and as the POH/AFM says (ACS CA.IX.A.S2)
Orientation and recovery (S3)
Stay oriented, divide attention, and plan and fly a smooth recovery (ACS CA.IX.A.S3)
Bank (S4)
Between 30 and 45 degrees, to keep the load factor positive (ACS CA.IX.A.S4)
Speed and level-off (S5)
Airspeed +0/-10 knots; level off at the specified altitude within 100 feet (ACS CA.IX.A.S5)
Checklists and SRM (S6, S7)
Complete the right checklists; use SRM (ACS CA.IX.A.S6, S7)

body.p: Private and commercial compared: the knowledge, risk and skill lines for bank, airspeed and level-off are word for word the same (ACS PA.IX.A.S4, S5; ACS CA.IX.A.S4, S5). The only change is that the private Task has a separate 'make radio calls as appropriate' element (ACS PA.IX.A.S7), and the commercial Task does not; it ends with SRM (ACS CA.IX.A.S7). So the commercial bar is not tighter numbers. It is deeper understanding: why the limits are where they are, and judgment about the whole emergency.

callout.text: Plus zero, minus ten. The target speed is a ceiling, not a center. Anything above it is out of tolerance (ACS CA.IX.A.S5).
The POH/AFM procedure comes first. If the AFH guidance conflicts with the manufacturer's procedure for your airplane, the manufacturer's procedure takes precedence [[24:350|AFH 18-1]].

check.q: Your POH emergency descent procedure differs from the AFH's generic guidance. Which one do you fly?
check.a: The manufacturer's procedure. The AFH says its emergency guidance does not replace the AFM/POH, and the manufacturer's procedure takes precedence if they conflict [[24:350|AFH 18-1]].

chunks.title: Why get down now: fire, smoke, decompression and medical problems

body.p: Each trigger has its own reason for leaving altitude. Knowing the reason tells you how fast you really need to go and where the descent should end.

head: Trigger
Why altitude is the enemy
What the sources say to do
rows: Engine compartment fire
Even a brief, intense fire can damage the structure, and the airplane may still be burning out of sight [[24:359|AFH 18-10]]
Fuel off unless the POH says otherwise; a single-engine airplane without power has to make a forced landing [[24:358|AFH 18-9]] [[24:359|AFH 18-10]]
Severe cabin smoke (unpressurized)
Smoke and fumes harm everyone aboard and hide the panel
Oxygen masks if you have them, and start an immediate descent [[24:359|AFH 18-10]]
Intense smoke (pressurized)
The pressurization air normally clears smoke, but not intense smoke
Depressurize at altitude if everyone has oxygen, or make an emergency descent [[24:359|AFH 18-10]]
Decompression
The main danger is hypoxia; decompression sickness is another [[1:197|PHAK 7-37]]
Rapid descent from altitude is necessary [[1:197|PHAK 7-37]]
Altitude decompression sickness
Nitrogen bubbles form in the body at low pressure [[1:440|PHAK 17-18]]
Oxygen, emergency descent, land as soon as possible [[1:440|PHAK 17-18]]
Hypoxia
Judgment and coordination fail, often without the pilot noticing [[1:426|PHAK 17-4]]
Fly lower and/or use supplemental oxygen [[1:426|PHAK 17-4]]

body.p: Engine fire, one detail that matters for speed: fires that seemed to be out have been known to start again when the airflow pattern and airspeed change [[24:359|AFH 18-10]]. A high-speed descent might blow the fire out, but weakened structure is a major concern, and a slower descent puts less stress on it [[24:357|AFH 18-8]]. Keep in mind that the airplane is expendable; only the people aboard matter [[24:359|AFH 18-10]].

Medical problems: for altitude decompression sickness the PHAK lists oxygen at 100 percent, an emergency descent, and a landing as soon as possible. Even if the symptoms go away on the way down, land and get a medical evaluation; symptoms can also show up later on the ground [[1:440|PHAK 17-18]]. For other medical emergencies, such as a passenger who becomes ill, the sources do not set a procedure. Whether to descend fast is your judgment (application: a rapid descent helps only when altitude is part of the problem; a quick landing helps in almost every case).

callout.text: Ask early. An aircraft is in at least an urgency condition the moment the pilot is doubtful about anything that could affect safety, and that is the time to ask for help [[34:28|AIM 6-1-2]].

check.q: A passenger becomes ill at 9,500 ft in an unpressurized airplane. Do the sources give an emergency descent procedure for this?
check.a: No. The sources set no procedure for medical problems other than hypoxia and decompression sickness, so how fast to descend is your judgment (application: a quick landing helps in almost every case).

body.p: Many commercial jobs use pressurized airplanes, and the Pressurization lesson (CA.VIII.B) covers the system itself. Here is the part that leads to an emergency descent. Decompression means the system can no longer hold its designed pressure difference, because of a malfunction or structural damage [[1:196|PHAK 7-36]].

bullets: Explosive decompression: cabin pressure changes faster than the lungs can empty, which can damage the lungs. Anything under 0.5 seconds is usually considered explosive [[1:196|PHAK 7-36]].
Rapid decompression: the lungs empty faster than the cabin [[1:196|PHAK 7-36]].
Explosive decompression is more likely in small pressurized airplanes than in large ones; the risk of lung damage is much lower in a rapid decompression [[11:41|AC 61-107B 2-11a(3)]].
Signs: noise, a dazed moment, fog, dust or flying debris. The fog comes from the sudden drop in temperature and the change in humidity [[1:196|PHAK 7-36]].
Rapid decompression shortens your useful time, because oxygen is pushed out of the lungs [[1:196|PHAK 7-36]].
Structural damage adds the danger of being blown out near an opening, plus wind blast and extreme cold, so keep seatbelts on when pressurized [[1:197|PHAK 7-37]].

Slow decompression is as dangerous as, or more dangerous than, a rapid one, because it may go unnoticed while hypoxia dulls your mind [[11:28|AC 61-107B 2-7e(3)]]. The cabin altitude warning is often your only clue [[11:41|AC 61-107B 2-11a(3)]].

body.p: The cabin altimeter and the cabin rate-of-climb indicator tell you what the cabin is doing; the differential pressure gauge shows the difference between inside and outside pressure [[1:196|PHAK 7-36]]. All pressurized aircraft have automatic visual and aural warnings [[1:197|PHAK 7-37]].

Time of useful consciousness falls fast with altitude: 3 to 5 minutes at 25,000 ft and 1 to 2 minutes at 30,000 ft in the PHAK table [[1:426|PHAK 17-4]]. A rapid decompression cuts it by at least 50 percent [[11:30|AC 61-107B 2-7e(3)]]; the AC table shows 1.5 to 2.5 minutes at 25,000 ft after one [[11:29|AC 61-107B Figure 2-3]]. It is not the time until you pass out: impaired performance may start at once [[11:28|AC 61-107B 2-7e(3)]]. That is why oxygen comes before anything else, and the descent second.

callout.text: For 20,000 ft, the AIM says the ability to take corrective and protective action is lost in 5 to 12 minutes [[34:182|AIM 8-1-2]], not the 30 minutes or more shown in the PHAK table [[1:426|PHAK 17-4]]. Plan with the AIM number.

Pressurized airplanes above FL 250 must carry at least a 10-minute oxygen supply for each occupant, beyond any other required oxygen, for a descent after a loss of cabin pressure [[60:491|14 CFR 91.211(b)]]. Above 15,000 ft cabin altitude, every occupant must be provided with oxygen [[60:491|14 CFR 91.211(a)]].

No oxygen after a decompression, or hypoxia suspected without a working mask: make an emergency descent to below 10,000 ft MSL, and land as soon as possible if the symptoms persist [[11:42|AC 61-107B 2-11a(4)]].

check.q: Why should passengers seated next to a window or door keep their seatbelts fastened the whole time the cabin is pressurized?
check.a: A decompression from structural damage can toss or blow people near an opening out of the airplane, and expose them to wind blast and extreme cold [[1:197|PHAK 7-37]].

body.p: In an emergency you cannot always read a checklist first. The ACS expects you to do the published or recommended immediate action memory items, then review the checklist once conditions allow (Commercial ACS, Appendix 2). Learn your airplane's emergency descent, fire and smoke memory items cold.

bullets: Engine fire: unless the POH says otherwise, mixture to idle cutoff and fuel selector OFF, ignition left ON to burn the fuel left in the lines. If the flames go out, do not restart [[24:358|AFH 18-9]].
Electrical fire: try to find and isolate the faulty circuit. If you cannot, and conditions permit, turn the battery master and alternator off; burning materials may keep burning [[24:359|AFH 18-10]].
Before the master goes off for anything but an electrical fire or an imminent crash landing, remember you lose the panel radios and ATC loses your transponder [[24:358|AFH 18-9]].
Turning circuits back on one at a time to find the bad one recreates the original problem. The most prudent course is to land as soon as possible [[24:359|AFH 18-10]].
Cabin fire: fight the fire and get on the ground as quickly as possible [[24:359|AFH 18-10]].

body.p: Rules and ATC: in an in-flight emergency that needs immediate action, the pilot in command may deviate from any rule of part 91 to the extent required, and must send a written report if the FAA asks [[60:435|14 CFR 91.3]]. If you leave an ATC clearance to do that, tell ATC as soon as possible and get an amended clearance [[34:28|AIM 6-1-1]].

The AIM's list of actions for any distress also says to climb, if possible, for better communication and radar coverage [[34:45|AIM 6-3-2]]. With fire, smoke or a decompression, getting down comes first (application). Talk on the way down, and remember MAYDAY commands radio silence on the frequency [[34:45|AIM 6-3-1]].

callout.text: Commercial habit: say your immediate actions out loud as you do them. It keeps you in order under stress and shows the examiner your sequence (ACS CA.IX.A.S6).

check.q: You call MAYDAY on Center's frequency. What does that word do to everyone else on the frequency?
check.a: It commands radio silence on that frequency; distress calls have absolute priority [[34:45|AIM 6-3-1]].

chunks.title: Airspeed limits: which number is your ceiling?

body.p: The AFH says to fly the descent at the maximum allowable airspeed for the procedure you use, never past VNE, VLE or VFE as they apply, and inside VA in turbulence [[24:357|AFH 18-8]]. Your real ceiling is the lowest limit that applies at that moment.

head: Limit
Where you find it
What it protects
rows: VNE (red line)
Marked on the airspeed indicator
Above it, damage or structural failure may result [[1:211|PHAK 8-9]]
VNO (top of green arc)
Marked; the yellow arc runs from VNO to VNE
Above it, fly only in smooth air and with caution [[1:211|PHAK 8-9]]
VFE (top of white arc)
Marked
Maximum speed with flaps extended [[1:211|PHAK 8-9]]
VLE and VLO
Placards and the POH, not the dial
Top speed with the gear extended, and for moving the gear [[1:212|PHAK 8-10]]
VA
Placards and the POH, not the dial
Rough-air speed and top speed for abrupt control use [[24:389|AFH G-17]] [[1:212|PHAK 8-10]]

body.p: Rough air changes everything. VNE is set for smooth air only, and gust loads grow with airspeed [[1:134|PHAK 5-37]]. In extremely rough air, slow to the design maneuvering speed, and know that some gusts can exceed the load limits at any speed [[1:134|PHAK 5-37]]. Most POHs now include turbulent air penetration information; use it [[1:134|PHAK 5-37]].

VA moves with weight. It might be 100 knots heavy and only 90 knots light [[1:212|PHAK 8-10]]. A pilot descending alone with little fuel has a lower VA than the placard for maximum weight. For older airplanes with no published VA, it is about 1.7 times the normal stall speed [[1:132|PHAK 5-35]].

How turbulence shows up: in moderate turbulence the airspeed usually varies; in severe turbulence it varies a lot and the airplane may be out of control for a moment [[34:106|AIM TBL 7-1-11]]. With a +0 tolerance (ACS CA.IX.A.S5), aim a little below your ceiling so the swings stay under it (application).

callout.text: You must follow the operating limits in the approved flight manual, markings and placards [[60:436|14 CFR 91.9]]. An emergency allows you to deviate from rules where needed, but the airframe does not know it is an emergency.

check.q: Smooth air, clean airplane, and your POH emergency descent speed puts you in the yellow arc. Is that allowed?
check.a: Yes. The yellow arc is for smooth air only, and with caution [[1:211|PHAK 8-9]]. If it turns bumpy, slow down toward VA or the POH turbulence speed [[1:134|PHAK 5-37]].

chunks.title: Configuring for drag: power, propeller, gear and flaps

body.p: Fly the configuration and speeds the manufacturer recommends [[24:357|AFH 18-8]]. Unless the manufacturer prohibits it:

bullets: Power to idle [[24:357|AFH 18-8]].
Propeller control (if you have one) to low pitch, high rpm. The propeller then acts as an aerodynamic brake and helps stop the speed from running away [[24:357|AFH 18-8]].
Gear and flaps as the manufacturer recommends, for maximum drag, so you can descend fast without excessive speed [[24:357|AFH 18-8]].

body.p: The AFH gives two general pictures. Chapter 18 speaks of extending gear and flaps as recommended [[24:357|AFH 18-8]]. Chapter 3 says emergency descents are generally high-drag, high-speed procedures, with an example configuration of idle power, propellers forward, gear extended and flaps retracted, at a specific speed [[24:82|AFH 3-21]]. Both point to the POH. Why flaps are often left up: VFE is usually far lower than VLE or VNE, so extending flaps lowers your speed ceiling (application).

head: Situation
Configuration trade-off
rows: Cabin smoke
On some airplanes, lowering the gear and/or flaps can make a cabin smoke problem worse [[24:359|AFH 18-10]]
Flaps extended
Flaps bring lower design G-load limits, which is why accelerated stalls are never practiced with flaps out [[24:124|AFH 5-19]]. Pull gently in the recovery
Engine fire
High speed may blow it out, but low speed is easier on a structure that fire may have weakened [[24:357|AFH 18-8]]
Long descent in a piston engine
Prolonged practice can overcool the cylinders [[24:358|AFH 18-9]]; high-speed descents can shock cool the engine [[1:177|PHAK 7-17]]

callout.text: Retractable gear: VLO limits gear movement and VLE limits flight with it down [[1:212|PHAK 8-10]]. Slow below VLO before you lower the gear; then, if your VLE is higher, the POH may let you speed up to it.
The examiner gives the scenario, and you pick the configuration from it (ACS CA.IX.A.S2). Say why: 'Smoke, so gear down per the POH but flaps stay up.'

check.q: Why is the propeller set to high rpm in the descent?
check.a: The low pitch, high rpm propeller acts as an aerodynamic brake and helps prevent too much airspeed buildup [[24:357|AFH 18-8]].

chunks.title: Structural limits: limit load, ultimate load and the Vg diagram

body.p: Load factor is the ratio of lift to weight. Pull 3 G and the structure carries three times the airplane's weight; it also raises the stall speed [[1:130|PHAK 5-33]]. Designers plan for the highest loads expected in normal use, called limit loads [[1:130|PHAK 5-33]].

bullets: Limit load: the structure must carry it without detrimental permanent deformation and without interfering with safe operation [[60:107|14 CFR 23.2235]].

Ultimate load: the limit load times a 1.5 factor of safety [[60:106|14 CFR 23.2230]]. Parts may bend or twist at these loads, and that reserve is for the unexpected, not for regular use [[1:130|PHAK 5-33]].
Category limit load factors in the PHAK: normal +3.8 to -1.52, utility +4.4 to -1.76, acrobatic +6.0 to -3.0. Airplanes over 4,000 lb have lower limits [[1:131|PHAK 5-34]].
Operating above the positive limit load can cause objectionable permanent deformation and a high rate of fatigue damage [[1:134|PHAK 5-37]].

body.p: Read the Vg diagram from left to right. The curved line is the most lift the wing can make at each speed; above it the wing stalls [[1:134|PHAK 5-37]]. Where that curve meets the limit load factor is the maneuvering speed. Below it, the airplane stalls before it can make a damaging positive load [[1:134|PHAK 5-37]]. The vertical line at VNE is the limit airspeed; past it, structural damage or failure may result from a variety of causes [[1:135|PHAK 5-38]].

An emergency descent pushes you to the right side of this chart, the fast side. There, the same pull on the yoke makes far more G than it would at slow speed, and gusts hit harder [[1:134|PHAK 5-37]]. That is why the recovery has to be gentle.

callout.text: VA is not a shield against everything. Below VA you are protected only for one full control input, one time, in one axis, in smooth air; it gives no protection against several full inputs in one axis or full inputs in more than one axis at once [[1:132|PHAK 5-35]]. Rapid, large alternating inputs may cause structural failure at any speed, even below VA [[1:133|PHAK 5-36]] [[13:8|AC 61-67C 100f]].

check.q: The 1.5 factor of safety means the structure holds well past the limit load. Can you plan to use that reserve in a hard pull-out?
check.a: No. The strength reserve is not something to abuse; it is there for unexpected conditions [[1:130|PHAK 5-33]]. Above the limit load, permanent deformation and fatigue damage can happen [[1:134|PHAK 5-37]].

chunks.title: Why 30 to 45 degrees of bank: keep the G positive

body.p: The ACS asks for 30 to 45 degrees of bank to keep the load factor positive (ACS CA.IX.A.S4), and the AFH gives the same range for the same reason [[24:357|AFH 18-8]].

The problem with pushing straight over: snapping the elevator forward can reduce the load factor toward zero or below, the feeling of floating or rising from the seat [[1:133|PHAK 5-36]]. The negative limits are much smaller than the positive ones, for example -1.52 against +3.8 in the normal category [[1:131|PHAK 5-34]]. Rolling into a bank and letting the nose come down in the turn gets the airplane headed down while you keep a little back pressure, so the G stays positive (application).

Why not steeper than 45 degrees: load factors grow quickly and start to matter for both performance and the wing structure past about 45 degrees [[1:133|PHAK 5-36]]. In a level turn, 45 degrees means 1.41 G and 60 degrees means 2 G [[24:211|AFH 10-2]].

More G also means a higher stall speed. Stall speed rises with the square root of the load factor [[24:211|AFH 10-2]] [[13:8|AC 61-67C 100g]]. The chart shows the idea: at 3 G, an airplane that stalls at 45 knots in level flight will stall at about 75 knots [[1:132|PHAK 5-35]]. That is far below emergency descent speeds, but it matters if you pull hard while slowing down in the recovery.

callout.text: Hold a constant bank, coordinated, and let pitch and drag set the speed. If the bank creeps past 45 degrees, the nose drops and the speed jumps toward your ceiling. Watch the bank as closely as the airspeed (ACS CA.IX.A.S4, S5).

check.q: Why is a sharp push-over a poor way to start the descent?
check.a: It can drive the load factor toward zero or negative [[1:133|PHAK 5-36]], and the negative limit load factors are much smaller than the positive ones [[1:131|PHAK 5-34]].

chunks.title: The recovery: lead it, roll level, raise the nose gently

body.p: Start the recovery high enough to get back to level flight, or to a precautionary landing, safely [[24:357|AFH 18-8]]. In training, once the descent is established and stable, end it [[24:358|AFH 18-9]].

The lead: for a 1,000 fpm descent the AFH starts the level-off 100 ft, 10 percent of the descent rate, above the target [[24:82|AFH 3-21]]. Emergency descent rates are much higher, so the lead is bigger. The AFH gives no special lead for this maneuver; the 10 percent rule is a starting point (application).

Pulling out at high speed is where airframes get overloaded. Abrupt pull-ups at high diving speeds can impose critical loads [[1:133|PHAK 5-36]]. A rolling pull-out exceeds the design limit more easily, so roll the wings level first [[24:131|AFH 5-26]]. Near VNE, make control inputs slowly and gently [[24:131|AFH 5-26]]. The spiral dive recovery template below is written for an upset, but its order teaches the same lesson.

bullets: Wings level, coordinated, then ease the nose up to the level attitude (application, following [[24:131|AFH 5-26]]).
If flaps are out, be extra gentle: their design G limits are lower [[24:124|AFH 5-19]].
Add power as the speed comes back, and clean up the gear and flaps within VLO and VFE [[1:212|PHAK 8-10]].
Hold the specified altitude within 100 ft (ACS CA.IX.A.S5).
Watch engine temperatures after a long idle descent; high-speed descents can shock cool the engine [[1:177|PHAK 7-17]].

callout.text: A startled pilot who yanks back and rolls level at the same time can create loads that damage or break the airframe [[24:131|AFH 5-26]]. Plan the recovery before you start down.

check.q: You are descending at 2,000 fpm toward a 4,000 ft level-off. Using the AFH 10 percent rule as a starting point, where do you begin the level-off?
check.a: 10 percent of 2,000 fpm is 200 ft, so start at about 4,200 ft [[24:82|AFH 3-21]]. The AFH gives the rule for a 1,000 fpm descent, so treat it as a minimum and lead more if needed (application).

chunks.title: Where you are going: altitude, wind, terrain and the landing spot

body.p: An emergency descent ends in one of two places: a safe lower altitude, or the ground. Decide which before you start down, and keep updating it as you go.

bullets: Single-engine fire with the fuel off: there is no choice but a forced landing [[24:359|AFH 18-10]]. Pick the field early.
Smoke, decompression or medical: a precautionary landing at an airport is usually less hazardous than a forced landing, because you have time to choose and power to fix errors [[24:350|AFH 18-1]].

Gliding distance: a 10 to 1 glide ratio means 10,000 ft forward for every 1,000 ft down [[24:82|AFH 3-21]]. An emergency descent at high speed covers much less ground than a best glide, so the reachable area shrinks fast (application).

Terrain and obstructions: the level-off altitude must clear them. On the checkride the examiner specifies it (ACS CA.IX.A.S5); in real life you choose it, and start the lead early enough to hold it (application).

body.p: Wind and landing distance: the speed that counts at touchdown is groundspeed. Doubling it quadruples the destructive energy [[24:352|AFH 18-3]], so land into the wind. Very little stopping distance is needed if the deceleration is even; at a uniform 9 G, 50 mph needs about 9.4 ft [[24:352|AFH 18-3]]. Dense crops, brush and small trees can absorb energy [[24:351|AFH 18-2]].
Watch your own mind: reluctance to accept the emergency, undue fear, and the wish to save the airplane all lead to delays and bad choices [[24:350|AFH 18-1]] [[24:351|AFH 18-2]].

callout.text: Down to what? Before the nose goes down, name the destination: an altitude, an airport, or a field.

check.q: Why is a precautionary landing usually less hazardous than a forced landing?
check.a: You have more time to choose the terrain and plan the approach, and you can use power to make up for errors [[24:350|AFH 18-1]].

body.p: You are about to drop through thousands of feet of airspace in a minute or two. Every altitude you pass may hold traffic you never saw.

bullets: Clear the area before the maneuver. Clearing turns make sure the next maneuver does not go into another aircraft's flightpath, and good clearing plus a good scan is the most effective collision defense [[24:33|AFH 1-12]].
The turn itself lets you check for traffic below and look for a landing area [[24:357|AFH 18-8]].
A radio call announcing your descent may be appropriate to warn others [[24:357|AFH 18-8]].
See and avoid applies to everyone, IFR or VFR, whenever weather permits [[60:447|14 CFR 91.113(b)]].
An aircraft in distress has the right-of-way over all other traffic [[60:447|14 CFR 91.113(c)]], but other pilots can give way only if they see you (application).
Transponder: keep your assigned code while in contact with ATC; if you cannot reach ATC right away, squawk 7700 [[34:46|AIM 6-3-2]].

callout.text: Some airplanes have Emergency Autoland, which can make its own emergency descent. These systems take no evasive action against other aircraft, so avoid the path of any airplane you think may be under one [[24:33|AFH 1-12]] [[24:371|AFH 18-22]].
On the checkride, clear out loud: 'Clear left, clear right, clear below.' In a high-wing, raise the wing to look under it before you roll in (application).

check.q: Under 14 CFR 91.113, who has the right-of-way when you are in distress, and does that make you safe?
check.a: You do, over all other traffic [[60:447|14 CFR 91.113(c)]]. It does not make you safe: others can only give way if they see you, so you still clear and scan [[60:447|14 CFR 91.113(b)]].

body.p: Fire, smoke, noise, scared passengers and a steep descending turn all at once is a recipe for losing the picture. The examiner will add realistic distractions on purpose to see how you divide your attention (Commercial ACS, Appendix 2).

bullets: Coriolis illusion: after a turn long enough for the inner-ear fluid to catch up, a head movement in another plane can create a strong false sense of turning [[1:429|PHAK 17-7]]. Reaching to the floor for a fire extinguisher or a fuel selector in a long descending turn is exactly that. Move your head as little as possible [[1:429|PHAK 17-7]].
The leans: rolling out after a long turn can make you feel banked the other way [[1:429|PHAK 17-7]]. Trust the instruments, especially if smoke or haze hides the horizon.
Hypoxia can give a false sense of security, so you may feel fine while your judgment is failing [[1:426|PHAK 17-4]].
Stress can make you breathe faster and hyperventilate, with symptoms much like hypoxia. Slow your breathing or talk aloud [[1:426|PHAK 17-4]] [[1:427|PHAK 17-5]].

body.p: SRM is using every resource on board and outside: ATC, the autopilot, other people [[1:43|PHAK 2-4]]. Fly first; then use your helpers. A passenger can watch for traffic or hold the checklist (application). Never let ATC or passengers make risk decisions for you [[1:43|PHAK 2-4]].

callout.text: Positive exchange of flight controls: 'You have the flight controls.' 'I have the flight controls.' 'You have the flight controls,' with a visual check. There should never be doubt about who is flying (Commercial ACS, Appendix 2).

check.q: In the middle of the emergency you notice you are breathing fast and your fingers tingle, though the cabin is low. What is likely, and what helps?
check.a: Hyperventilation from stress [[1:426|PHAK 17-4]]. Slow your breathing rate; talking aloud also helps [[1:427|PHAK 17-5]].

chunks.title: Fly it step by step (and what the examiner checks)

body.p: A generic flow. Your POH gives the real speeds, configuration and memory items.

bullets: 1. Before flight: brief the POH emergency descent speed and configuration, VNE, VNO, VFE, VLE, VLO and VA at today's weight [[1:211|PHAK 8-9]] [[1:212|PHAK 8-10]].
2. Listen to the scenario. Name the trigger and the destination, an altitude or a landing spot (ACS CA.IX.A.S2).
3. Clear the area, including below [[24:33|AFH 1-12]] [[24:357|AFH 18-8]].
4. Immediate actions for the scenario (fuel off, smoke, oxygen), then the emergency descent: power idle, propeller high rpm, gear and flaps per the POH [[24:357|AFH 18-8]].
5. Roll into 30 to 45 degrees of bank and let the nose come down; keep the G positive (ACS CA.IX.A.S4).
6. Hold the maximum allowable airspeed for the configuration and the air: +0/-10 knots (ACS CA.IX.A.S5) [[24:357|AFH 18-8]].
7. Radio call and transponder as appropriate; keep scanning [[24:357|AFH 18-8]] [[34:46|AIM 6-3-2]].
8. Run or review the checklist once the descent is stable (Commercial ACS, Appendix 2).
9. Lead the level-off, roll wings level, raise the nose gently, and level within 100 ft of the specified altitude [[24:82|AFH 3-21]] [[24:131|AFH 5-26]] (ACS CA.IX.A.S5).
10. Power and cleanup within the limits; watch engine temperatures [[1:177|PHAK 7-17]].

head: Fault the examiner sees
Why it fails
rows: Airspeed 2 knots over the target
+0 means no overshoot (ACS CA.IX.A.S5)
Bank of 25 or 55 degrees
Outside 30 to 45 degrees (ACS CA.IX.A.S4)
Level-off 150 ft low
Outside 100 ft (ACS CA.IX.A.S5)
No clearing before rolling in
S1 (ACS CA.IX.A.S1)
Flaps out above VFE
Configuration and airspeed not per the POH (ACS CA.IX.A.S2)

check.q: In this flow, when do you read the checklist itself?
check.a: After the memory items, once the descent is stable and conditions permit; if reading it is unsafe or impractical, the examiner looks at your memory items and later review (Commercial ACS, Appendix 2).

body.p: The AFH has no common-errors list for this maneuver. These come from its emergency descent text, the load factor material and the ACS.

head: Error
Fix
rows: Aiming at the ceiling speed and drifting over it
Aim slightly below the ceiling, more so in bumpy air [[1:134|PHAK 5-37]] (ACS CA.IX.A.S5)
Forgetting VA drops at light weight
Brief VA for today's weight [[1:212|PHAK 8-10]]
Flaps extended out of habit, then flying past VFE
Use the POH configuration; if flaps are out, VFE is the ceiling [[24:357|AFH 18-8]]
Pushing over hard to start down
Roll into the bank and let the nose fall; keep the G positive [[24:357|AFH 18-8]] [[1:133|PHAK 5-36]]
Bank creeping past 45 degrees
Fix bank first; the speed follows (ACS CA.IX.A.S4)
Late level-off and a hard pull
Lead the level-off; roll level, then ease the nose up [[24:82|AFH 3-21]] [[24:131|AFH 5-26]]
Head down in the checklist during the turn
Memory items first, eyes outside, checklist when stable (Commercial ACS, Appendix 2) [[1:429|PHAK 17-7]]
Holding the descent too long in practice
Establish, stabilize, then end it to protect the engine [[24:358|AFH 18-9]]

callout.text: Fly a practice descent with your CFI calling out bank and airspeed every few seconds, then do one silently. The difference shows where your scan breaks down.

check.q: Why does the AFH say to end a practice emergency descent once it is established and stable?
check.a: Prolonged practice can cool the engine cylinders too much in a piston airplane [[24:358|AFH 18-9]].

f1.caption: Figure 18-6. Emergency descent. (AFH 18-9)
f1.alt: A high-wing airplane in a steep left bank begins a curving descent, shown by an orange path sweeping down and away over green farm fields, a road with utility poles, a farmhouse and distant brown hills.

f2.caption: Figure 5-55. Typical Vg diagram. (PHAK 5-38)
f2.alt: A graph of load factor from -3 to 7 against indicated airspeed from 0 to 240 mph. A curved accelerated stall line rises from the normal stall speed at 1 G to the maneuvering speed at about 4.4 G. A green normal operating range runs to the maximum structural cruise speed, then a yellow caution range runs to the never-exceed speed. Orange structural damage zones lie above the positive limit and below the negative limit, and red structural failure lies beyond.

f3.caption: Figure 5-54. Load factor changes stall speed. (PHAK 5-35)
f3.alt: Two linked charts. On the left, a curve shows the ratio of accelerated to normal stall speed rising with G load, with a dashed line from 3 G up to a ratio of about 1.7. On the right, red lines for normal stall speeds of 40 to 150 knots convert that ratio to an accelerated stall speed, with the dashed line ending near 75 knots.

f4.caption: Figure 5-18. Spiral dive recovery template. (AFH 5-27)
f4.alt: A five-step table: 1, reduce power to idle; 2, apply some forward elevator; 3, roll wings level; 4, gently raise the nose to level flight; 5, increase power to climb power.

f5.caption: Figure 7-42. Cabin pressurization instruments. (PHAK 7-36)
f5.alt: Two round gauges. Left, a cabin rate-of-climb indicator in thousands of feet per minute. Right, a combined gauge with an outer cabin altitude scale in thousands of feet and an inner differential pressure scale in psi, with a red arc marking the maximum differential pressure limit.

f6.caption: Figure 17-1. Time of useful consciousness. (PHAK 17-4)
f6.alt: A table. 45,000 ft MSL: 9 to 15 seconds. 40,000 ft: 15 to 20 seconds. 35,000 ft: 30 to 60 seconds. 30,000 ft: 1 to 2 minutes. 28,000 ft: 2.5 to 3 minutes. 25,000 ft: 3 to 5 minutes. 22,000 ft: 5 to 10 minutes. 20,000 ft: 30 minutes or more.

scenario.title: Bang at FL 220
scenario.setup: You are a commercial pilot flying a pressurized single-engine piston airplane on a positioning flight at FL 220, IFR, in contact with Center. A company mechanic rides in the back. Below is flat terrain with a minimum en route altitude of 9,000 ft, and the tops of a cloud layer are at 8,000 ft. There is a loud bang, the cabin fills with fog, your ears pop, and the cabin altitude needle is climbing fast.

questions.q: The cabin altitude is climbing fast. Why does AC 61-107B say a small cabin like yours leaves less time than an airliner with the same size hole?
questions.a: A small cabin volume decompresses faster: under the same conditions a small pressurized airplane can decompress 10 to 200 times faster than a large one, so the crew is likely to have less time for lifesaving actions [[11:41|AC 61-107B 2-11a(2)]].

questions.q: Mask on, you pull the power to idle for the descent. What engine risk does AC 61-107B name, and does it change your plan?
questions.a: A high-altitude rapid descent can cold-shock a piston engine and crack cylinders, but reaching a safe altitude is the top priority [[11:42|AC 61-107B 2-11a(4)]]. Fly the AFM descent and watch engine temperatures on the way down [[1:177|PHAK 7-17]].

questions.q: You are IFR at FL 220. May you leave your altitude before ATC clears you, and what about the transponder?
questions.a: Yes. In an emergency needing immediate action you may deviate from part 91 rules as needed [[60:435|14 CFR 91.3]], then tell ATC as soon as possible and get an amended clearance [[34:28|AIM 6-1-1]]. Keep the assigned code while in contact; 7700 only if you cannot reach ATC [[34:46|AIM 6-3-2]].

questions.q: How do you configure and what speed do you fly, given that a window or door may have failed?
questions.a: Follow the AFM emergency descent: idle, propeller high rpm, gear and flaps as recommended, at the maximum allowable speed within VNE, VLE and VFE [[24:357|AFH 18-8]]. If you suspect structural damage, the AFH logic for fire damage applies: lower speeds put less stress on the structure [[24:357|AFH 18-8]], and the airplane may be harder to control [[24:359|AFH 18-10]].

Below 12,500 ft the crew oxygen rule no longer applies [[60:491|14 CFR 91.211(a)]]. The AC 61-107B hypoxia procedure says to descend, preferably below 10,000 ft [[11:27|AC 61-107B Table 2-6]], and the AIM encourages oxygen above 10,000 ft in the day [[34:183|AIM 8-1-2]]. The MEA is 9,000 ft and the tops are at 8,000 ft, so 9,000 ft with an ATC clearance meets all of these (application). Lead the level-off [[24:82|AFH 3-21]].

questions.q: Level at 9,000 ft, Center asks your intentions. Your destination is 150 NM away and an airport is 20 NM away. What do you do?
questions.a: Plan to land soon at the near airport. A precautionary landing at an airport is generally less hazardous than waiting until it becomes a forced landing [[24:350|AFH 18-1]], the airplane may be damaged [[24:359|AFH 18-10]], and decompression sickness symptoms can appear later, even on the ground [[1:440|PHAK 17-18]] (application).

skills.do: Clear the area, including below, before rolling into the descent.
skills.practice: Do clearing turns before every practice descent and say 'clear below' out loud [[24:33|AFH 1-12]] [[24:357|AFH 18-8]].

skills.do: Set the airspeed and configuration that fit the examiner's scenario and the POH/AFM.
skills.practice: Have your CFI give a different trigger each time (engine fire, cabin smoke, decompression) and say your configuration and why before you start [[24:357|AFH 18-8]] [[24:359|AFH 18-10]].

skills.do: Stay oriented, divide attention, and plan and fly a smooth recovery.
skills.practice: Brief the level-off altitude and lead before rolling in; on recovery roll level first, then ease the nose up [[24:82|AFH 3-21]] [[24:131|AFH 5-26]].

skills.do: Hold a bank between 30 and 45 degrees to keep the load factor positive.
skills.practice: Aim for about 40 degrees so small errors stay inside the 30 to 45 degree window (application) [[24:357|AFH 18-8]].

skills.do: Hold the right airspeed with no overshoot and up to 10 knots slow, and level off within 100 ft of the specified altitude.
skills.practice: Brief the ceiling speed for the configuration and the air, then aim a few knots below it [[1:134|PHAK 5-37]] [[1:211|PHAK 8-9]].

skills.do: Do the immediate action items, then complete the right checklists.
skills.practice: Say your memory items aloud, then pull the checklist once stable (Commercial ACS, Appendix 2).

skills.do: Use SRM: use ATC, the autopilot and passengers well, and keep decisions your own.
skills.practice: In scenario flights, brief a passenger to watch for traffic and practice short, clear ATC calls on the way down [[1:43|PHAK 2-4]] [[34:28|AIM 6-1-1]].

quiz.q: How do the commercial skill standards for this Task differ from the private ones?
options: The commercial Task has no separate radio-call element; the bank, airspeed and altitude standards are the same
The commercial airspeed tolerance is +0/-5 knots
The commercial bank range is 45 to 60 degrees
The commercial level-off tolerance is 50 feet
quiz.why: Private S7 is 'make radio calls as appropriate' (ACS PA.IX.A.S7); the commercial Task has no such element and ends with SRM (ACS CA.IX.A.S7). Bank, airspeed and level-off lines are identical (ACS PA.IX.A.S4, S5; ACS CA.IX.A.S4, S5).

quiz.q: Thick black smoke, not bright orange flames, pours from the engine cowling. What does the AFH say this points to, and what extra step may help?
options: A fuel-fed fire; open the cowl flaps
An oil-fed fire; consider stopping the propeller so the engine-driven pump stops feeding it
An electrical fire; turn the master off
Carburetor ice; apply carburetor heat
quiz.why: Thick black smoke suggests an oil-fed fire, while a fuel-fed fire makes bright orange flames. The AFH says to consider stopping the propeller, by feathering or by low rpm and raising the nose, so the oil pump stops feeding the fire [[24:358|AFH 18-9]].

quiz.q: What is the primary danger of a decompression?
options: Hypoxia
Ear pain
Engine overspeed
Fog in the cabin
quiz.why: The primary danger of decompression is hypoxia; decompression sickness is another [[1:197|PHAK 7-37]]. Fog is a normal sign of it [[1:196|PHAK 7-36]].

quiz.q: Why might you hold off on turning the master switch off during an engine fire?
options: It shuts off the fuel pump
Unless the fire is electrical or a crash is imminent, it kills the radios and ATC loses your transponder
It feathers the propeller
It stops the flaps from extending
quiz.why: Unless the fire is electrical or a crash landing is imminent, turning off the electrical system prevents panel radio use and causes ATC to lose transponder returns [[24:358|AFH 18-9]].

quiz.q: What is usually the first sign of an electrical fire?
options: Rising oil temperature
The distinct smell of burning insulation
A rough-running engine
A low-voltage light only
quiz.why: The initial indication of an electrical fire is usually the distinct odor of burning insulation [[24:359|AFH 18-10]].

quiz.q: According to the AFH, cabin fires generally come from which three sources?
options: Careless smoking, electrical malfunctions and heating system malfunctions
Fuel leaks, oil leaks and hydraulic leaks
Lightning, static and oxygen bottles
Landing lights, pitot heat and the starter
quiz.why: Cabin fires generally result from careless smoking, electrical system malfunctions or heating system malfunctions [[24:359|AFH 18-10]].

quiz.q: Another airplane nearby is descending under an Emergency Autoland system. What should you do?
options: Hold your course; it will turn away from you
Avoid its path, because these systems take no evasive action against other aircraft
Fly close to check on the pilot
Climb directly above it
quiz.why: Emergency Autoland systems take no evasive action against other aircraft, so avoid the path of any airplane under one, or suspected to be [[24:33|AFH 1-12]]. The system can fly its own emergency descent [[24:371|AFH 18-22]].

quiz.q: Why is flying a practice descent with flaps extended a reason to be gentle in the pull-out?
options: Flaps raise VNE
Flaps lower the design G-load limits
Flaps make the propeller overspeed
Flaps reverse the elevator
quiz.why: The AFH warns against accelerated stalls with flaps extended because of the lower design G-load limits in that configuration [[24:124|AFH 5-19]].

quiz.q: In a level turn, how much load factor does 45 degrees of bank produce?
quiz.why: A level 45 degree banked turn produces a load factor of 1.41; 60 degrees produces 2.0 [[24:211|AFH 10-2]].

quiz.q: When does the AIM say an aircraft is in at least an urgency condition?
options: Only after an engine failure
Only when the pilot has declared MAYDAY
The moment the pilot becomes doubtful about anything that could adversely affect flight safety
When ATC says so
quiz.why: An aircraft is in at least an urgency condition the moment the pilot is doubtful about position, fuel, weather or any other condition that could adversely affect flight safety; that is the time to ask for help [[34:28|AIM 6-1-2]].

final_quiz.q: You shut off the fuel for an engine fire, the flames disappear, and you think about diving at high speed to reach a runway 15 miles away. What does the AFH warn about?
options: Fires that appear to be out can rekindle with changes in airflow and airspeed, and fire may have weakened the structure
High speed always puts the fire out for good
The engine should be restarted to reach the runway
Fire cannot damage the wing structure in a single
final_quiz.why: Engine fires that seemed out have been known to rekindle with airflow and airspeed changes, and the structure may be damaged [[24:359|AFH 18-10]]. Low speed puts less stress on weakened structure [[24:357|AFH 18-8]]. Without power, a single must make a forced landing [[24:359|AFH 18-10]].

final_quiz.q: The examiner specifies a target of 140 knots and a level-off at 4,000 ft. Which performance meets the commercial ACS?
options: 132 to 139 knots, bank 35 to 45 degrees, leveled at 4,080 ft
136 to 142 knots, bank 35 to 40 degrees, leveled at 4,000 ft
131 to 138 knots, bank 25 to 35 degrees, leveled at 3,960 ft
134 to 140 knots, bank 40 degrees, leveled at 3,880 ft
final_quiz.why: Airspeed must be +0/-10 (130 to 140 knots), bank 30 to 45 degrees, and level-off within 100 ft (ACS CA.IX.A.S4, S5). Option two exceeds 140, option three's bank drops below 30, option four is 120 ft low.

final_quiz.q: You are at 160 KIAS, gear up, and your POH emergency descent calls for gear down. VLO is 130, VLE is 150 and VNE is 190. What is the right sequence?
options: Lower the gear now; VLE is above VLO
Slow below 130 to lower the gear, then hold no more than 150 (and the POH speed) with it down
Leave the gear up and dive to 190
Lower the gear at 160 and slow to 150 afterward
final_quiz.why: VLO is the top speed for moving the gear, and VLE the top speed with it extended [[1:212|PHAK 8-10]]. Never pass VLE once it is down [[24:357|AFH 18-8]]. At 160 you are above both.

final_quiz.q: After a decompression at FL 200, your oxygen mask will not work and you start to feel lightheaded. What does AC 61-107B say to do?
options: Stay at altitude and troubleshoot the mask
Make an emergency descent to below 10,000 ft MSL and land as soon as possible if symptoms persist
Descend slowly at 500 fpm to protect your ears
Climb to get above the problem
final_quiz.why: If supplemental oxygen is not available, initiate an emergency descent to an altitude below 10,000 ft MSL; if symptoms persist, land as soon as possible [[11:42|AC 61-107B 2-11a(4)]].

final_quiz.q: Fuel off, the engine fire is out, but the cowling is blistered. The owner on board says the bean field ahead will wreck the airplane and asks you to stretch for an airport 12 NM away. What do the AFH points support?
options: Stretch the glide; the airplane is valuable
Treat the airplane as expendable: it may be badly damaged or still burning, and only the people aboard matter
Restart the engine to reach the airport
Dive at high speed to reach the airport before the fire returns
final_quiz.why: The AFH says the airplane may be structurally damaged or still on fire, and it is expendable; only the safety of those aboard matters [[24:359|AFH 18-10]]. The desire to save the airplane leads to stretching glides and other bad choices [[24:351|AFH 18-2]].

final_quiz.q: During a recovery you see 4.2 G on an accelerometer in a normal category airplane with a +3.8 G limit. What is the situation?
options: No concern; the structure is good to 3.8 x 1.5 = 5.7 G
Beyond limit load: objectionable permanent deformation and fatigue damage are possible even though nothing broke
The airplane has passed its ultimate load and has failed
Only negative G can damage the airframe
final_quiz.why: Above the positive limit load factor, objectionable permanent deformation and a high rate of fatigue damage may occur [[1:134|PHAK 5-37]]. The 1.5 factor of safety is a reserve for the unexpected, not for use [[60:106|14 CFR 23.2230]] [[1:130|PHAK 5-33]].

final_quiz.q: In the recovery from a fast descending turn, the speed is near VNE and you have just rolled the wings level. How do you raise the nose?
options: Briskly, to stop the speed from building
Slowly and gently, because control inputs near VNE can cause structural failure
While adding full power at once
Push forward first, then pull hard
final_quiz.why: The airplane may be at or beyond VNE, so control inputs are made slowly and gently to prevent structural failure [[24:131|AFH 5-26]]. Abrupt pull-ups at high diving speeds can impose critical loads [[1:133|PHAK 5-36]].

final_quiz.q: Smoke comes from under the panel. You have a fire extinguisher and want to clear the cabin by opening the air vents. What does the AFH say comes first?
options: Open the vents first so you can see
Use the fire extinguisher, then open the vents to purge the smoke
Lower the gear to vent the cabin
Turn the cabin heat to full
final_quiz.why: Opening the cabin air vents to remove smoke should be done only after the fire extinguisher (if available) is used; close them at once if the smoke gets worse [[24:359|AFH 18-10]].

final_quiz.q: At 12,000 ft without oxygen, a passenger becomes giddy and his lips look blue. What is the right treatment?
options: Have him breathe into a bag
Descend to a lower altitude
Climb to get above the haze
Open the cabin heat
final_quiz.why: Euphoria and cyanosis are hypoxia symptoms, and treatment is flying at lower altitudes and/or using supplemental oxygen [[1:426|PHAK 17-4]].

final_quiz.q: After 3 minutes in a descending left turn through haze, you roll wings level and feel banked to the right. What should you do?
options: Bank left to feel level
Trust the attitude indicator; it is the leans
Pull back to stop the descent
Close your eyes until it passes
final_quiz.why: Leveling the wings after a prolonged turn can give the illusion of banking the other way, the leans [[1:429|PHAK 17-7]]. With a poor horizon, fly by the instruments.

final_quiz.q: PHAK 5-37 says no combination of maneuver and gust can cause damage below maneuvering speed. Which statement fits all the sources?
options: Below VA nothing can damage the airplane
VA covers one full input in one axis in smooth air; rapid alternating inputs, or some gusts, can exceed the limits even below it
VA only matters above 10,000 ft
VA protects only in turbulence, not in smooth air
final_quiz.why: The same PHAK page says some gusts can exceed load limits at any speed [[1:134|PHAK 5-37]]. VA covers one full input, one time, one axis, smooth air [[1:132|PHAK 5-35]], and alternating inputs may cause failure even below VA [[1:133|PHAK 5-36]] [[13:8|AC 61-67C 100f]].

final_quiz.q: After a decompression you put on your mask and breathe 100 percent oxygen. For a few seconds you feel worse, not better. What does AC 61-107B say?
options: Take the mask off; the oxygen is bad
Keep breathing 100 percent oxygen slowly; an apparent increase in symptoms for 15 to 60 seconds can happen
Switch to the cabin air setting
Hold your breath until it passes
final_quiz.why: After a severe hypoxia exposure, 100 percent oxygen can cause an apparent increase in symptoms for 15 to 60 seconds. The recovery stays the same: breathe 100 percent oxygen, slowly [[11:42|AC 61-107B 2-11a(4)]].

final_quiz.q: Smoke is thickening. Center asks you to hold your altitude for a few minutes because of traffic below. What does good SRM look like?
options: Hold altitude; ATC decides
Declare an emergency, say you are descending now, and let ATC move the traffic
Ask a passenger whether to descend
Turn off the radio to reduce workload
final_quiz.why: You are PIC; never let ATC or passengers make risk decisions for you [[1:43|PHAK 2-4]]. In an emergency you may deviate as needed [[60:435|14 CFR 91.3]], then tell ATC and get an amended clearance [[34:28|AIM 6-1-1]].

takeaways: Fire, smoke, decompression or a medical problem: get down fast, but never past a structural limit.
Your ceiling is the lowest limit that applies: VNE, VFE, VLE, or VA in rough air, and VA drops with weight.
Commercial standards: 30 to 45 degrees of bank, airspeed +0/-10 knots, level-off within 100 ft.
Bank to start down so the G stays positive; negative limits are much smaller.
Decompression: oxygen first, then the descent.
Lead the level-off, roll wings level, then raise the nose gently.
Clear below, name your destination, use ATC and passengers, and keep the decisions yours.
cfi_notes: The commercial bank, airspeed and level-off standards are identical to private (ACS PA.IX.A.S4, S5; CA.IX.A.S4, S5). Raise the bar in the oral: Vg diagram, limit and ultimate loads, VA and weight, and why the bank keeps G positive.

PHAK 5-37 describes the limit load as a force that bends the structure so it does not return to its original shape, and the ultimate load as the point of structural failure [[1:134|PHAK 5-37]]. Current 14 CFR 23.2235 requires the structure to carry limit loads without detrimental permanent deformation, and to support ultimate loads [[60:107|14 CFR 23.2235]]. Teach the CFR meaning; PHAK 5-37 itself places permanent deformation above the limit load in its Vg discussion.

For 20,000 ft, PHAK Figure 17-1 gives 30 minutes or more of useful consciousness [[1:426|PHAK 17-4]]; AIM 8-1-2 says corrective action is lost in 5 to 12 minutes [[34:182|AIM 8-1-2]]. AC 61-107B Figure 2-3 has no 20,000 ft row but gives 20 to 30 minutes at 18,000 ft [[11:29|AC 61-107B Figure 2-3]]. Teach the AIM number.

PHAK 5-37 says no combination of maneuver and gust can cause damage below maneuver speed, yet the same page says some gusts can exceed load limits at any speed [[1:134|PHAK 5-37]], and PHAK 5-36 and AC 61-67C say rapid alternating inputs may cause failure even below VA [[1:133|PHAK 5-36]] [[13:8|AC 61-67C 100f]]. Teach the version with the limits.

The PHAK category table (+3.8, +4.4, +6.0) [[1:131|PHAK 5-34]] reflects the older category system; current 14 CFR part 23 sets the 1.5 factor of safety [[60:106|14 CFR 23.2230]] but no category G numbers. Students should read their own POH limitations section.

AFH 18-8 speaks of gear and flaps extended as recommended, while AFH 3-21 gives flaps retracted as the typical example [[24:357|AFH 18-8]] [[24:82|AFH 3-21]]. They are not in conflict; both defer to the POH. Ask the student to explain why VFE often argues for flaps up.

AIM 6-3-2 tells pilots in distress to climb if possible for better communication [[34:45|AIM 6-3-2]]. Point out that in fire, smoke or decompression the descent wins; that judgment is the commercial-level point.

Brief simulated radio calls and who controls the throttle before the flight, and use the positive exchange of controls (Commercial ACS, Appendix 2). End each practice descent once it is stable to protect the engine [[24:358|AFH 18-9]]. In a pressurized airplane, simulate the decompression; never actually depressurize for training, and coordinate with ATC first [[11:45|AC 61-107B 2-12f]].

Keep this Task separate from the steep spiral (CA.V.B): different purpose, bank range and speed. The spiral dive template is used here only for its lesson about rolling level before pulling [[24:131|AFH 5-26]].
gaps: The emergency descent speed, configuration, gear and flap limits, VA at different weights and any turbulent air penetration speed come only from the POH/AFM.
The sources give load factors for level turns only; none gives the load factor in a descending turn or in the pull-out from an emergency descent.
The 10 percent level-off lead comes from a 1,000 fpm partial-power descent [[24:82|AFH 3-21]]; no source gives a lead for high-rate emergency descents.
The sources give no procedure for medical emergencies other than decompression sickness and hypoxia; whether to descend fast for an ill passenger is pilot judgment.
No source here says whether VNE or other limit speeds change with altitude, or gives propeller rpm limits for the descent; check the POH.
No source gives a decompression procedure for a specific pressurized single; use the AFM and the Pressurization lesson (CA.VIII.B).

steps: Check circuit breakers, instruments, avionics and lights for the faulty circuit
Turn the needed switches on one at a time, pausing to check for odor, smoke or sparks

activities.title: True or false: fire and decompression
activities.intro: Decide if each statement is true or false.

cards.s: Explosive decompression is more likely in a small pressurized airplane than in a large one.
cards.why: True. AC 61-107B says this type is more likely in small-volume pressurized aircraft [[11:41|AC 61-107B 2-11a(3)]].

cards.s: A rapid decompression carries a higher risk of lung damage than an explosive one.
cards.why: False. In a rapid decompression the risk of lung damage is significantly lower than in an explosive one [[11:41|AC 61-107B 2-11a(3)]].

cards.s: Time of useful consciousness is the time until you pass out, so you are fully capable until then.
cards.why: False. TUC does not mean the onset of unconsciousness; impaired performance may be immediate [[11:28|AC 61-107B 2-7e(3)]].

cards.s: As cabin pressure drops in a decompression, trapped gas expands, most noticeably in the ears and the stomach and intestines.
cards.why: True. Gas expansion with decreasing pressure is most noticeable in the ears and the GI tract [[11:28|AC 61-107B 2-7e(2)]].

cards.s: If an engine fire goes out after the fuel is shut off, restart the engine to reach an airport.
cards.why: False. If the flames are snuffed out, no attempt should be made to restart the engine [[24:358|AFH 18-9]].

cards.s: In a single-engine airplane, a fire can keep burning under the cowling where the pilot cannot see it.

activities.title: Work the descent numbers
activities.intro: Work it out, then type your answer.

items.q: The AFH says that at a uniform 9 G, stopping from 50 mph takes about 9.4 ft and from 100 mph about 37.6 ft, four times as far. Distance grows with the square of groundspeed. About how far at 70 mph?
items.why: 9.4 x (70 / 50) squared = 9.4 x 1.96 = 18.4 ft [[24:352|AFH 18-3]]. Lower groundspeed at touchdown, such as landing into the wind, pays off fast.

items.q: An older airplane has no published VA and stalls at 62 knots. Using the PHAK rule of thumb, about what is VA?
items.why: For older airplanes VA is about 1.7 times the normal stall speed: 62 x 1.7 = 105.4 knots [[1:132|PHAK 5-35]]. Always use the POH value when there is one.

items.q: A normal category airplane has a +3.8 G limit load factor. What ultimate load factor must its structure support?
The examiner gives a target of 140 knots. In the bumps the needle swings about 4 knots each way. What is the highest target that keeps every swing within +0 knots?
items.why: +0/-10 means 130 to 140 knots (ACS CA.IX.A.S5). 140 - 4 = 136, and the low swings, 136 - 4 = 132, stay above 130 (application).

items.q: Engine fire, fuel off, at 7,500 ft AGL. With a 10 to 1 glide ratio, how far could you glide at best glide in nautical miles (6,076.1 ft per NM)?
items.why: 7,500 x 10 = 75,000 ft forward [[24:82|AFH 3-21]]. 75,000 / 6,076.1 = 12.3 NM [[1:398|PHAK 16-11]]. A fast emergency descent covers far less ground.

activities.title: Smoke over the hills, one decision at a time
activities.intro: You are flying a retractable single at 10,500 ft MSL over hilly terrain, about 2,500 ft elevation, with two passengers on a commercial photo flight. The nearest airport is 18 NM ahead. POH emergency descent: idle, propeller high rpm, gear down, flaps up, 140 KIAS (VLE). VFE is 110 and VA is 118 KIAS at maximum weight; you are well below maximum weight.

steps.s: A burning smell and a light haze come from the cabin heat outlet.
options: Open the cabin heat fully to clear the haze
Shut off the cabin heat, the likely source, and watch the smoke
Start an emergency descent at VNE right away
Open all vents and ignore it if it fades
steps.why: Cabin fires often come from heating system malfunctions, and smoke is controlled by identifying and shutting down the faulty system [[24:359|AFH 18-10]].

steps.s: The smoke gets thicker and a passenger is coughing. You open the fresh air vent and the smoke increases.
options: Leave the vent open to purge the smoke
Close the vent and begin an immediate descent
Climb for better radio coverage first
Continue at altitude to the airport
steps.why: If smoke increases when the vents are opened, close them at once; with severe smoke, start an immediate descent [[24:359|AFH 18-10]]. Getting down comes before the AIM advice to climb for communications [[34:45|AIM 6-3-2]] (application).

steps.s: You start down. How do you configure?
options: Idle, propeller high rpm, gear down, flaps up, aiming a few knots under 140
Gear down and full flaps at 140 for maximum drag
Gear up, flaps up, at VNE
Cruise power to reach the airport sooner
steps.why: Use the POH configuration [[24:357|AFH 18-8]]. Flaps at 140 would exceed VFE 110 [[1:211|PHAK 8-9]] and can make cabin smoke worse [[24:359|AFH 18-10]]. With +0/-10, aim under the ceiling (ACS CA.IX.A.S5).

steps.s: Passing 7,000 ft you enter moderate turbulence and the airspeed swings about 10 knots.
options: Hold 140; VLE allows it
Slow below VA, which is less than 118 at your light weight, and accept a slower descent
Speed up to get through it quickly
Level off and wait for smooth air
steps.why: In rough air slow to maneuvering speed [[1:134|PHAK 5-37]], and VA is lower at light weight [[1:212|PHAK 8-10]]. Moderate turbulence usually causes airspeed variations [[34:106|AIM TBL 7-1-11]].

steps.s: With the heater off the smoke slowly clears. You are at 4,500 ft, 10 NM from the airport, over open farmland.
options: Turn the heater back on to confirm it was the source
Continue to the airport and land, ready to use a field if the smoke returns
Land in the nearest field right now
Climb back up and finish the photo flight
steps.why: A cabin fire means getting on the ground as quickly as possible [[24:359|AFH 18-10]], and a precautionary landing at an airport is less hazardous than a forced landing [[24:350|AFH 18-1]]. Turning a suspect system back on invites the original problem again (application, by analogy with the AFH electrical fire note [[24:359|AFH 18-10]]).
